newsitem.title: UK: Mexican growth underlines lure of Latam vs Asia.
newsitem.headline: Mexican growth underlines lure of Latam vs Asia.

text.p: Sparkling growth figures from Mexico, the best since 1981, highlight the appeal of Latin American asset markets over troubled southeast Asia, analysts said on Tuesday.
"Latin America is a solid, bullish story which underlines the volatility in Asia," said Neil Williams, economist at Sumitomo Bank in London.
Data released on Monday showed Mexico's gross domestic product (GDP) leapt 8.8 percent year-on-year, beating forecasts and buoying confidence in its equity and debt markets.
Strong growth is seen as a plus both for companies and government revenues.

The Mexican story is in sharp contrast to the picture in Asia where two months of currency turmoil have pushed up interest rates, cut growth prospects, stoked inflation fears and threatened corporate earnings.
Ironically, Mexico's current strength stems from its ability to bounce back from the far worse peso crisis of 1994.
"It's the culmination of the rebound from the 1995 recession. Mexico is now reaping the reward of a very tough orthodox adjustment programme," said Peter West, chief economist at BBV LatInvest.

Morgan Stanley Dean Witter echoed the view of others in tipping South America as the key target for emerging market funds in the face of the continuing currency uncertainty stemming from the fall of the Thai baht.
"Latin America looks better and better, and remains likely to trade to a premium over Asia over the next 12 months," it said in a briefing note.
The current pause in Latin American stocks, notably Brazil where currency worries have unsettled some investors, was a buying opportunity, it said.
Funds have steered clear of Asia in view of recent currency uncertainty, but for many this is part of a longer-term preference for the South American "puma" over the Asian "tiger".
"Latin America, although it has performed well this year, still looks extremely attractive," said James Graham-Maw, global portfolio manager at Foreign and Colonial Emerging Markets.

He singled out continuing reforms in countries such as Venezuela, Brazil and Argentina together with a sharp improvement in foreign direct investment since the Mexican peso crisis as underpinning current optimism.
Some contrarians argue the time may be approaching to shift funds back to Asia, anticipating that currency devaluation will boost exports and hence stock markets in Asia in the long term.

"Generally we have been overweight Latin America and underweight Asia since the start of the year and I don't see any reason to shift that around dramatically," said Nigel Rendell, emerging market strategist at HSBC James Capel.
"But there are still certain countries in the Far East which we think are reasonable, and some people might want to start to buy places like Thailand now that most of the bad news is out of the way."
But Graham-Maw believes a move back into Asian assets -- significantly cheaper now than a couple of months ago -- is premature.
"When economies go through these transitions the dust takes an awfully long time to settle," he said.

Foreign and Colonial Emerging Markets Investment Trust had a weighting of 49 percent to Latin America, 28 to Europe, Middle East and Africa, 18 percent to Asia and five percent to others at the end of July.
